0.title: Holy, Holy, Holy Is the Lord
0.essay:
Only one attribute of God is ever repeated three times in a row in Scripture. The Bible never says God is “love, love, love” or “mercy, mercy, mercy”. But twice — once in Isaiah’s vision and once in John’s — the creatures nearest the throne cry, “Holy, holy, holy” (Isaiah 6:3; Revelation 4:8). And they never stop.

Everything he is

Holiness is not one quality of God among others. It describes everything he is. His love is holy love; his power is holy power; his justice, mercy and wisdom are all holy. To say that God is holy is to say that he is God — utterly unlike anything he has made, and utterly pure.

What we lose, and what we regain

Our age has largely lost sight of this. God is often imagined as a helpful friend, a life coach or a kindly grandfather. He is kind beyond imagining, but he is never ordinary. And when God’s holiness fades from view, everything fades with it: sin seems small, grace unremarkable, the cross unnecessary, worship casual and holiness of life optional.

The opposite is also true. When God’s holiness comes back into view, everything changes. Sin is seen for what it is. Grace becomes amazing. The cross becomes the place where holiness and love meet. Worship becomes awe. And the call to be holy becomes not a burden but a privilege: to be made like the most beautiful being there is.

The chapters

What It Means That God Is Holy; Holiness Revealed — approaching a holy God; Holiness and Sin; Holiness and the Cross; Be Holy, for I Am Holy; and Worship and Glory — holiness for ever. This study belongs with the Fear of the Lord and Biblical Wisdom: God’s holiness is why we fear him, and the fear of him is the beginning of wisdom.

1.title: What It Means That God Is Holy
1.essay:
At its root, “holy” means set apart. When Scripture calls God holy, it means two things above all: he is set apart in majesty, and set apart in purity. And then it tells us something astonishing — that this God draws near to the lowly.

Set apart in majesty

God is the Creator, and everything else is creature. He is not the highest being on a scale that includes us; he is in a category of his own. After the crossing of the Red Sea, Israel sang, “Who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? Who is like you, majestic in holiness, awesome in glorious deeds, doing wonders?” (Exodus 15:11). The question expects the answer: no one. Hannah prayed, “There is none holy like the LORD: for there is none besides you” (1 Samuel 2:2). Worship begins when we stop comparing God with anything else.

Isaiah 40 was written to exiles who felt forgotten and small. God answered them not by making himself smaller but by showing how great he is — measuring the waters in his hand, calling the stars by name, holding the nations like a drop in a bucket — and then asking, “To whom then will you compare me, that I should be like him? says the Holy One” (Isaiah 40:25). The comfort of God’s people is that their God has no equal. And the incomparable one “gives power to the faint” (Isaiah 40:29).

Set apart in purity

God is perfectly good, without the smallest trace of evil, selfishness or deceit. Habakkuk says, “You who are of purer eyes than to see evil and cannot look at wrong” (Habakkuk 1:13). His holiness is not merely the absence of sin but the fullness of goodness — a blazing moral beauty. And it is not our purity at its best, only bigger. It is the purity of the one who is himself the standard of goodness.

The Holy One draws near

Here is the wonder. “For thus says the One who is high and lifted up, who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy: ‘I dwell in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit’” (Isaiah 57:15). The holiest being in the universe makes his home with broken, humble people. Holiness does not keep God away from the lowly; it keeps him away from the proud. The way into God’s presence is down, not up.

In Hosea, holiness is even the reason for mercy. Israel had been unfaithful again and again, yet God says, “I will not execute my burning anger… for I am God and not a man, the Holy One in your midst” (Hosea 11:9). A man wronged so often would give up. God is not a man. He does not forgive the way we forgive, grudgingly and partially; he forgives as God.

Holiness is God’s Godness

Holiness is not an item on a list beside love, power and wisdom; it is the quality of all of them. God’s love is holy, so it is never sentimental or indulgent. His power is holy, so it is never cruel or arbitrary. His justice is holy, so it is never vindictive.

Isaiah’s favourite name for God is “the Holy One of Israel”. It joins two things we might keep apart: God’s infinite otherness and his covenant closeness. “Your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel” (Isaiah 41:14). And holiness is the shared life of the triune God: the Father is “Holy Father” (John 17:11), the Son is “the Holy One of God” (John 6:69), and the Spirit is the Holy Spirit.

That is why Jesus taught us to begin our prayers, “Hallowed be your name” (Matthew 6:9). Before we ask for bread, forgiveness or protection, we ask that God be treated as holy — in our lives and in all the world.

A bigger God

When God first spoke to Moses from the burning bush, his first instruction was not about Egypt or Pharaoh: “Take your sandals off your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground” (Exodus 3:5). Ordinary desert became holy because God was there.

A Christian’s picture of God had shrunk over years of busyness. Prayer had become a list of requests; Bible reading a quick devotional thought. Then, reading Isaiah slowly, he began to see God’s greatness and purity again. His prayers started with adoration. His sins troubled him more, and his forgiveness amazed him more. Nothing in his circumstances had changed. His view of God had.

For reflection

When you think of God, what comes to mind first? If it is only what he can do for you, ask him to show you more of his holiness. How does Isaiah 57:15 change the way you think about approaching a holy God? What would it look like to pray “hallowed be your name” this week and mean it?

2.title: Holiness Revealed: Approaching a Holy God
2.essay:
The Old Testament teaches God’s holiness not only in words but in arrangements: boundaries around a mountain, curtains in a tent, priests and blood. Every one of them said the same thing — God is holy, and sinners cannot simply walk into his presence. And every one of them was waiting for something better.

Boundaries, curtains and blood

At Mount Sinai God told Moses to set limits around the mountain: “Take care not to go up into the mountain or touch the edge of it” (Exodus 19:12). God was coming near, and his nearness was dangerous. Then God gave the tabernacle, whose whole design taught holiness: an outer court, then the Holy Place, then, behind a thick curtain, the Most Holy Place where the ark of the covenant stood. “The veil shall separate for you the Holy Place from the Most Holy” (Exodus 26:33). Only priests could enter the Holy Place; only the high priest could enter the Most Holy Place, once a year, on the Day of Atonement, “and not without taking blood” (Hebrews 9:7).

Hebrews says this arrangement was itself a message from the Holy Spirit: “the way into the holy places is not yet opened” (Hebrews 9:8). For centuries Israel’s worship said, “Not yet.” Every year the high priest went in and came out, and the curtain stayed in place.

Two shocking stories

Nadab and Abihu, sons of Aaron, had been on the mountain and seen God’s glory. They were ordained priests. Yet they “offered unauthorized fire before the LORD, which he had not commanded them. And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed them” (Leviticus 10:1–2). Their sin was not that they worshipped too much, but that they worshipped on their own terms. Moses explained it with God’s own words: “Among those who are near me I will be sanctified, and before all the people I will be glorified.” And Aaron, grieving two sons, “held his peace” (Leviticus 10:3). Some truths about God are too weighty for an immediate reply.

Later, when King David moved the ark on an ox-cart, the oxen stumbled and Uzzah reached out to steady it, “and God struck him down there because of his error” (2 Samuel 6:7). To many readers Uzzah seems to have done something good. But the whole procession was wrong from the start: God had commanded that the ark be carried on poles by Levites (Numbers 4:15; 1 Chronicles 15:13–15), not loaded on a cart like Philistine cargo. The story is not about a small slip, but about a people who had grown casual about the presence of God.

What they teach

These events seem harsh to modern readers. But they teach that God is not to be approached on our terms; he must be worshipped as he has commanded. Sincere intentions are not enough — Nadab and Abihu were priests; Uzzah meant well. This is one reason Reformed churches have taken care to shape their worship by Scripture. And the closer people are to God, the more seriously they must take his holiness. Privilege brings responsibility.

When the men of Beth-shemesh looked into the ark and were struck down, they asked, “Who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God?” (1 Samuel 6:20). It is the great question of the Old Testament. They were right that no sinner can. But they asked it in fear, wanting God to go away. The gospel asks the same question and gives a different answer.

Reverence and joy

After Uzzah’s death, David was afraid and angry, and left the ark with Obed-edom for three months. Then he learned. When he brought the ark to Jerusalem the second time, it was carried properly, with sacrifices, and David “danced before the LORD with all his might” (2 Samuel 6:14). He discovered that reverence and joy are not enemies. Joy that knows God is holy is deeper, not smaller.

Our worship today

A church that wanted to grow began shaping its services mainly around what visitors would enjoy — the music, the lighting, the length all designed for comfort. Nothing is wrong with welcoming outsiders. But the elders began asking a harder question: is our worship shaped by what God has commanded and by who he is? They kept their warmth, and recovered the reading of Scripture, the confession of sin and the prayers that reflect a holy God.

Leviticus 10 still speaks to the believer who drifts into casual worship — arriving late, scrolling a phone during prayer, singing words without thinking. Those who are near God must treat him as holy. And yet the curtains and the blood were shadows. They pointed forward to the day when the true High Priest would offer the true sacrifice, and the curtain would be torn from top to bottom.

For reflection

What did the tabernacle teach Israel about God, and what does it teach you? Why do you think God judged Nadab, Abihu and Uzzah so severely, and how do these stories make you feel? David learned to combine reverence and joy: which do you most need to grow in?

3.title: Holiness and Sin
3.essay:
God’s holiness is the measure by which sin is seen for what it is. When we compare ourselves with other people, we often look quite good. When we compare ourselves with God, there is no comparison at all.

On their faces

That is why Scripture’s great encounters with God’s holiness end with people on their faces. Isaiah cried, “Woe is me! For I am lost” (Isaiah 6:5). Ezekiel saw the glory of the LORD and “fell on my face” (Ezekiel 1:28). Manoah said, “We shall surely die, for we have seen God” (Judges 13:22).

Job had argued for chapters that he did not deserve his suffering, and in a sense he was right. But when God spoke from the whirlwind, Job did not win the argument. He worshipped: “I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you; therefore I despise myself, and repent in dust and ashes” (Job 42:5–6). That does not mean he hated himself in an unhealthy way. He saw himself rightly next to God, and turned from complaint to worship. Real encounters with God’s holiness always produce humility — and humility is the doorway to restoration (Job 42:10).

What sin is

Sin is not merely breaking rules or failing to reach our potential. It is rebellion against the holy God. After his adultery and murder, David prayed, “Against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight” (Psalm 51:4). He had wronged others terribly, but the deepest offence of every sin is against God.

And sin creates a gulf. The people complained that God was not hearing their prayers; Isaiah answered, “your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God, and your sins have hidden his face from you” (Isaiah 59:2). Sin is not only a moral failure but a broken relationship. The only remedy is one that deals with the sin — and Isaiah goes on to promise a Redeemer who will come to Zion (Isaiah 59:20).

“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). God’s holiness is the standard, and no one meets it. The respectable and the notorious alike need mercy.

Holy wrath

God’s holiness responds to sin with wrath. “For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men” (Romans 1:18). Paul begins his explanation of the gospel with wrath, not because wrath matters more than love, but because no one understands the good news until they understand the bad news.

God’s wrath is not a loss of temper. It is the settled, righteous opposition of perfect goodness to evil — what holiness and love look like when they meet evil that destroys what God loves. A God indifferent to abuse, cruelty and injustice would not be good. Habakkuk wrestled with how a God “of purer eyes than to see evil” could seem to tolerate it (Habakkuk 1:13). His question rested on a true foundation: because God is holy, evil will not have the last word. That is the believer’s confidence in a wicked world.

Why this matters

If we do not understand God’s holiness, we will think sin is small and grace is ordinary. We will treat forgiveness as something God owes us. But when we see his holiness, we learn to say with Isaiah, “Woe is me” — and that is the first step toward hearing, “your guilt is taken away” (Isaiah 6:7).

When the Holy Spirit shows us our sin, it can be painful. But conviction is a mercy. Those who never feel the weight of sin never run to the Saviour. God humbles us in order to lift us up.

A respectable church member had always thought of himself as a good person. He did not lie, steal or cheat on his wife. Then, through a series of sermons on God’s holiness, he began to see the pride beneath his respectability, his impatience at home, his coldness toward God. For the first time he understood why he needed a Saviour and not just a moral example. It was the beginning of real joy.

And when a friend says, “A loving God wouldn’t judge anyone,” a wise answer is: would you really want a God who ignored evil? What would that say about the victims of injustice? God’s holiness and love meet at the cross, where he judges sin and saves sinners at the same time.

For reflection

Why do people who see God’s holiness fall on their faces? How does comparing yourself with others hide the seriousness of sin? Is it hard for you to think of God’s wrath as holy and good? Read Psalm 51: how does David’s view of sin reflect his view of God?

4.title: Holiness and the Cross
4.essay:
The deepest question of the Bible is this: how can a holy God welcome sinful people without ceasing to be holy? If he simply overlooked sin, he would not be just. If he simply punished it, no one would be saved. The answer is the cross.

The Holy One came

First, God sent his Son, who was himself perfectly holy. The angel told Mary, “the child to be born will be called holy—the Son of God” (Luke 1:35). Even demons recognised him: “I know who you are—the Holy One of God” (Mark 1:24). Peter called him “the Holy and Righteous One” (Acts 3:14). He lived the holy life no one else had lived.

Hebrews describes him as the high priest we need: “holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners” (Hebrews 7:26). Israel’s high priests had to offer sacrifices for their own sins first; Jesus did not. Yet “separated from sinners” does not mean distant from them. He ate with sinners, touched lepers and welcomed outcasts. He was separated from sinners in character, not in compassion.

The great exchange

Then, on the cross, the Holy One took the place of the unholy. “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). Christ knew no sin, yet God treated him as the sin-bearer and poured out on him the judgment our sins deserved. His righteousness is counted as ours; our sin was counted as his.

God’s holiness was not set aside at the cross; it was fully displayed. For centuries God had passed over former sins without punishing them fully, which might have suggested he was indifferent to sin. The cross answers that. God put Christ forward “as a propitiation by his blood… to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:25–26). A propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away wrath. God himself provided the sacrifice that satisfies his own holiness. He is not a reluctant God who must be persuaded to love us; he is the loving God who paid the price his holiness required.

At the cross, God’s holiness is not softened by his love, and his love is not limited by his holiness. Both are displayed at full strength. It is the most holy and the most loving event in history.

The torn curtain

When Jesus died, “the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom” (Matthew 27:51). The barrier that had stood for centuries was opened — from God’s side. On the Day of Atonement, the high priest had gone behind the curtain with fear, carrying blood, and come out again, every year, because no sacrifice could finally take away sin. Now the work was finished.

“Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh… let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith” (Hebrews 10:19–22). His torn body is the torn curtain. The call is no longer “Keep away” but “Draw near.” God’s holiness has not changed. What has changed is that we come clothed in Christ.

The old question — “Who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God?” (1 Samuel 6:20) — has its answer. Those who are in Christ can stand, and more than stand. They can draw near.

Already holy in God’s sight

Believers are not only forgiven; they are declared righteous in Christ and set apart as God’s own. “And by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all” (Hebrews 10:10). In Christ we are already holy in God’s sight — and that is the foundation for growing in holiness. The way of approach is still through blood and a priest. But the blood is Christ’s, and the priest is Christ.

When guilt says “keep away”

A believer struggling with guilt over past sin felt unable to pray. “How can I come to a holy God after what I have done?” The answer is not to pretend God is less holy, but to look at the cross. God’s holiness has already dealt with that sin in Christ. The holiness that once barred the way now guarantees the welcome.

And when someone asks, “Why did Jesus have to die? Couldn’t God just forgive?”, a wise answer begins with God’s holiness. Forgiveness that ignored sin would make God unjust and sin unimportant. At the cross God forgave in a way that shows both how seriously he takes sin and how much he loves sinners.

For reflection

Why could God not simply overlook sin? Read Romans 3:21–26 slowly: what does it show about God’s holiness and love? How does the torn curtain change the way you pray? Is there a sin that makes you feel you cannot come to God, and what does the cross say to that feeling?

5.title: Be Holy, for I Am Holy
5.essay:
God’s holiness is not only something to admire. It is something he shares. “As he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct, since it is written, ‘You shall be holy, for I am holy’” (1 Peter 1:15–16).

The same call, new power

Peter grounds the call in two things: who called us, and who God is. And it reaches “all your conduct” — there is no area of life where holiness does not apply. He quotes Leviticus, where the command appears again and again (Leviticus 11:44; 19:2), because the call has not changed from the Old Testament to the New. What has changed is that Christ has redeemed us “with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:19) and given us his Spirit. The command is the same; the power to obey is new.

Holy already, and becoming holy

Scripture speaks of our holiness in two ways. First, believers are already holy in Christ. Paul lists sins that exclude people from God’s kingdom and then says, “And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:11). The Corinthian church included former idolaters, thieves, drunkards and the sexually immoral. All three verbs are past tense: before they had grown at all, God had made them his holy people. That is why the New Testament calls ordinary believers “saints” — holy ones. Theologians call this definitive sanctification.

Second, believers are being made holy, growing day by day in likeness to Christ: “For this is the will of God, your sanctification” (1 Thessalonians 4:3). This is progressive sanctification, the lifelong work of the Spirit (2 Corinthians 3:18). Both are God’s work, and both involve our active obedience. We become in practice what God has already made us in Christ.

No believer becomes sinless before glory. “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John 1:8). Holiness is real growth, not a claim to perfection — and the holiest Christians are often the most aware of their remaining sin.

What holiness looks like

Holiness is not strange clothes, withdrawal from society or a list of man-made rules. Leviticus 19, the chapter that says, “You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy” (Leviticus 19:2), is surprisingly earthy. It goes on to speak of honouring parents, leaving the edges of the harvest for the poor, paying workers on time, honest weights, justice for the deaf and blind, respect for the elderly, love for the foreigner — and at its centre, “you shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18), which Jesus called the second great commandment. Holiness is purity in body and mind, honesty in business, kindness in speech and love in action.

Joseph, tempted daily by his master’s wife, refused because it would be sin “against God” (Genesis 39:9); when she grabbed him, he ran. A young man struggling with pornography installs accountability software, gives a friend permission to ask hard questions and fills his evenings with better things; he fails sometimes and confesses quickly, and over months the grip loosens. A business owner discovers a supplier has undercharged her for months and pays what she owes, though no one would ever notice. A woman whose conversations slide into gossip decides that when someone’s name comes up, she will say something good or say nothing. And a Christian family tempted to withdraw from their neighbourhood stays, guards their home and loves their neighbours. Holiness is distinctness, not distance.

Driven by grace

Holiness is driven by grace, not fear of rejection. Paul appeals “by the mercies of God” (Romans 12:1). It is the grace of God that trains us “to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age” (Titus 2:12). We do not become holy to be accepted. We pursue holiness because we have been accepted.

God uses means: “Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth” (John 17:17). He makes us holy through his word, prayer, the fellowship of the church and the Lord’s Supper — and even through discipline and suffering, “that we may share his holiness” (Hebrews 12:10).

Holiness is necessary

“Strive for peace with everyone, and for the holiness without which no one will see the Lord” (Hebrews 12:14). We do not earn heaven by holiness; Christ alone is the ground of our salvation. But holiness is its evidence: those God saves, he makes holy, and it shows. The verse is also a promise. One day the holy people of God will see the Lord. Every step of holiness now is preparation for that sight.

For reflection

What is the difference between being holy in Christ and growing in holiness, and why do we need both? Read Leviticus 19: which of its practical commands most challenges you? Where is God calling you to grow in holiness right now — body, mind, speech, money or relationships?

6.title: Worship and Glory: Holiness Forever
6.essay:
God’s holiness is not only a truth to understand or a standard to live by. It is a beauty to worship. “Worship the LORD in the splendor of holiness; tremble before him, all the earth!” (Psalm 96:9).

The splendour of holiness

We sometimes think of holiness as strict and joyless. Scripture speaks of its splendour. Holiness is not cold and grey but radiant and glorious — the most beautiful thing in the universe. The right response to beauty this great is both joy and awe: “worship” and “tremble” side by side. And Psalm 96 calls all the earth to worship. God’s holiness is not a private matter for Israel or the church; every nation is called to bow before the Holy One, and one day every nation will.

Psalm 99 is a hymn to God’s holiness, ringing with a refrain: “Exalt the LORD our God; worship at his footstool! Holy is he!” (Psalm 99:5). Worship is the right response to holiness. When we see God as he is, we cannot help but praise him.

The song that never ends

In Revelation 4, John is taken into the throne room of heaven. The four living creatures, “full of eyes all around and within”, cry day and night, “Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!” (Revelation 4:8). They see everything, and what they see moves them to one unending cry. They are not bored or repeating a formula. Each time they look at God, they see more of his holiness, so they say it again. Heaven’s worship is not a ritual that grows stale; it is endless discovery of the infinite beauty of God. Eternity will not be long enough to explore it.

And the final song of the redeemed, from every nation, is about holiness: “Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy” (Revelation 15:4).

We shall see him

“We know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. And everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure” (1 John 3:2–3). The sight of God will complete our transformation. And the hope is not only future: those who expect to see the Holy One begin preparing now. Holiness in this life is rehearsal for eternity — learning to love now what we will love for ever.

God will finish what he began: “he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6). Christ reconciled us “in order to present you holy and blameless and above reproach before him” (Colossians 1:22).

A holy people in a holy city

The end of the story is a holy people in a holy city. “But nothing unclean will ever enter it” (Revelation 21:27). That is a warning — and for believers, a promise. Every sin that troubles us now will be gone. Christ will present his church “holy and without blemish” (Ephesians 5:27).

And even ordinary things will be holy. The high priest once wore a gold plate on his turban engraved “Holy to the LORD” (Exodus 28:36). Zechariah saw a day when “there shall be inscribed on the bells of the horses, ‘Holy to the LORD’” (Zechariah 14:20), and ordinary cooking pots would be as holy as the temple’s sacred bowls. The division between sacred and ordinary will disappear — not because holiness becomes common, but because everything becomes holy. Every part of life, work, home, rest and play will be holy to the Lord.

Holy in the ordinary

A mother of young children feels her days are anything but holy: nappies, meals, laundry and noise. Zechariah 14 speaks to her. Ordinary things done for the Lord are holy to him; the kitchen pot can be a vessel of worship.

A believer facing death reads Revelation 4 and 21. He knows he is not yet what he should be. But he knows he will see the Holy One and be made like him, and he is not afraid. The holiness that once would have condemned him is now his hope.

This week, read Psalm 99 or Revelation 4 aloud. Begin your prayers with praise for God’s holiness. Ask him to show you one area where he wants to make you more holy — and thank him that he will finish the work.

For reflection

Have you thought of God’s holiness as beautiful? What does heaven’s endless worship teach you about God? How does the hope of seeing him motivate you to pursue holiness now? What ordinary part of your life could you offer to God as “Holy to the LORD” this week?
